the runtime hands out no registration tokens: a park is the loop's, identified by core::net::ParkId, and an awaitable holds its own. Nothing a consumer writes names one.

the TUI keeps no registration list. co_await runtime.waitReadable(handle) parks on the loop, and the park is unregistered when the await resumes, ready or cancelled.

it became core::tui::runtime::TerminalInputSource (runtime/TerminalInputSource.hpp), an adapter with no wait: handles in, decoded events out. Both of its platform bodies are gone with it. Task B4. The one Async header that lands in core::net rather than core::async: IReactor's contract -- the turn, the park table, generation-checked cancellation and the ordered teardown -- became core::net::EventLoop, which owns an IoBackend. Its members are the FastCache::IReactor rows below. A file including it for the scheduling primitives alone (StopToken, ParkedWork, IExecutor) now wants the core/async header that holds the one it uses; this row names the whole-interface destination, which is where a caller of addTimer, submit or blockOn has to arrive.

Task B6. ISocket::IsClosed -> isClosed is recorded HERE rather than rewritten: the table keys a member row on (profile, name) and FastCache::AsyncQueue::IsClosed already holds it, the mirror of the Close collision that row records. Every other ISocket member B6 renamed has a row of its own: WriteVectored, WaitReadable, CancelRead, ShutdownWrite, SetReceiveDeadline, HandshakeIfNeeded and PeerAddress.

the shape changed with the name: attach() takes a ReadinessHandler whose callbacks the backend invokes, setInterest() is separate and reports the kernel's refusal as std::expected<void, NetError>, and wait() dispatches rather than returning a WaitOutcome

Task B8. Three changes a caller can see: host is std::string, not std::string_view (the task is lazy, so a view could dangle before the body copies it; a literal or a std::string compiles unchanged, a string_view argument becomes std::string { view }); a stop of the flow's own token throws core::async::OperationCancelled instead of returning NetErrorCode::Cancelled; an unresolvable name is NetErrorCode::AddressError. Resolution no longer runs on the loop's thread.
readiness is scripted against a HandlerId, handed out in attach order, in place of an FdToken; pushFailure() is new and models the hangup a kernel volunteers

Task B4. It parks on a HANDLE with a stated HandleKind rather than on a descriptor, because a Windows SOCKET and a waitable HANDLE reach different wait primitives and the backend cannot tell them apart from the value. endo's core::tui::runtime::WaitFdAwaiter is a different type and keeps its name until Task B12 removes it.
renamed so the row for the table it lives in reads as a table and not as a backend

Task B4. `detail`, because a consumer never names it: `EventLoop` holds one and answers `running()`, `isOnWorkerThread()` and `teardownIsSerialisedWithDispatch()` out of it. Its `Scope` nests here, which upstream's did not need.
Task B4. `clock()` is const and returns `core::platform::IClock&`; upstream's was non-const and returned FastCache's own IClock.

Task B4. `stop()` asks a `run()` to return and is safe from any thread; what upstream ALSO meant by Stop -- cancel every flow and unpark its waiters -- is `requestStop()` here, and the two are separated because a shutdown that only wants the loop back should not cancel work that is mid-flight.

Task B1. fastcached's SECOND SyncRun -- the overload taking a callable that retrieves the park -- is a name of its own here, core::async::syncRunWith(task, retrieve), declared in the same header. The table keys on the source symbol, so it cannot carry a second row: the rewrite turns every SyncRun into syncRun, and a two-argument call then fails to compile, which names the site to change by hand. That is deliberate -- the alternative is a call that compiles and means something else.

Task B1. An executor's parked-work entry; only an executor implementation names it.

Task B1. Header-only here: fastcached's ThreadPoolExecutor.cpp is inlined, so a consumer links nothing new for it. Not in the WebAssembly subset.

Task B1. It is built over core::async::IExecutor rather than fastcached's IReactor, so the constructor's first argument changes type: an EventLoop still satisfies it. Its members become camelBack -- push, pop, isClosed, size, hasWaiter, displaced, each a row below -- except Close: the table keys a member row on (profile, name) and ISocket::Close already holds it, so AsyncQueue::Close -> close is recorded here rather than rewritten. Its pop() is also stop-aware now: a cancel from the awaiting flow's own token throws core::async::OperationCancelled, where fastcached's could only answer nullopt on close.

Task B1. Its `bool accepted` is `AsyncQueueAdmission admission`: a bool result reporting success is a finding (.agent/rules/design-principles.md). No rewrite row, for the reason core::tui::LanguageId::Endo has none -- the TYPE changes with the name, so every use site needs a human: `if (queue.Push(x).accepted)` becomes `if (queue.push(x).admission == AsyncQueueAdmission::Accepted)`. `displaced` keeps its name and meaning.

Task B1. It also empties the task, which fastcached's does -- but here the awaiter takes the frame too, so a Task awaited with co_await std::move(t) is empty afterwards and t.handle(), t.done() and t.result() no longer answer about it.
Task B1. The table keys a member row on (profile, name), so this one row carries Submit for every executor: ThreadPoolExecutor's override and EventLoop's are the same rename.

a shape change, not a rename: the awaitable aggregate SleepUntil{&reactor, tp} becomes loop.sleepUntil(tp), or the free core::net::sleepUntil(&loop, tp) where the loop may be null -- the nullable-reactor contract upstream had. Task B5

a shape change: the aggregate takes the loop, the stop token and the deadline as arguments. Task B5: the wait no longer polls, so the fourth argument (wakeBound) is ignored -- the four-argument overload is kept for one release and then goes

Task B5. The arithmetic survives the rename; what it MEANS does not. Upstream called it the one place the polling rule is written down, and core-cpp no longer polls: interruptibleSleepUntil and DeadlineTimer park once and are woken. It is kept for a consumer still carrying a bounded wait of its own (RaftDriver, ExpiryReaper), and it goes when they do.
a shape change: SleepFor(reactor, delay) is the relative form, which is EventLoop::delay on the loop itself. Task B5

Task B5. The type survives; its implementation does not. Upstream was a detached coroutine polling a disarm flag over a shared_ptr<State> that outlived the timer so a late fire read live memory. EventLoop::cancelTimer retires the deadline by id, so there is no late fire, no shared state, no frame and no poll interval.

there is no poll to set an interval on (Task B5). Upstream's timer slept in 50ms steps re-reading a disarm flag, because a scheduled resumption could not be taken back; here an armed timer is what BOUNDS the loop's next wait, and disarming retires it. A caller passing the fifth constructor argument drops it; a caller that tuned it wanted a shorter reclaim latency, which is now zero turns.
*Listener::Bind(...) becomes the free function listen(loop, ListenOptions); the arguments regroup

a backend has no registration tokens any more: the ReadinessHandler's ADDRESS is its registration's identity, and detach() takes the handler. EventLoop keeps an id of its own for its parks (core::net::ParkId), which is internal to the loop.

Task B6. It is now an alias for core::net::ResultAwaitable<std::size_t>, so accept, handshake and fd-passing reads share one awaitable. A caller that only awaits one is unaffected; a caller that CONSTRUCTED one is not, because the suspend hook moved into the constructor -- see the removed rows for SetSuspendCallback and CallbackState.
Task B6. Public rather than a detail namespace: a transport outside this library is under the same one-read-operation rule, so it gets the same tripwire.

it returns ResultAwaitable<void> now, not void: a call in statement position becomes co_await sock->shutdownWrite(), with no write outstanding, and an override returns ResultAwaitable<void> and is no longer noexcept

Task B6: the hook moved into the constructor, because an awaitable that could be armed after it was built had a window in which it was neither ready nor arm-able and nothing said so. A transport now passes arm, retire and owner to ResultAwaitable(arm, retire, owner) -- and the RETIRE hook is new and mandatory: a flow whose stop token fires unwinds through await_resume, and a transport still holding a pointer to that operation would complete into a destroyed frame. A coroutine-shaped transport skips all three and uses ResultAwaitable(Task) instead.
Task B6: with the owner pointer passed at construction, the arm and retire hooks are handed it directly and nothing has to read it back off the awaitable.

Task B11: makeTlsServerContextFromFiles(certPath, keyPath) in core/net/Tls.hpp. It returns std::expected<std::shared_ptr<ITlsContext>, std::string> -- a construction failure is configuration, not a connection, so it is not a NetError -- and it serves every certificate in the file, intermediates included.

Task B11: makeSelfSignedServerContext(SelfSignedOptions{.commonName, .subjectNames, .validity}) in core/net/Tls.hpp. The common name is no longer hard-coded to "fastcache-node"; pass it. subjectNames is upstream's span of names, and an empty one means the common name alone. Task B11: no OpenSSL type crosses a core-cpp header (core-cpp.openssl-seam refuses one), so the SSL_CTX is not reachable. What callers used it for is on the interface: wrap() and certificateFingerprint().

Task B11: the TLS socket is private to core::net_tls. Wrap an accepted socket with ITlsContext::wrap or wrapTls, and await handshakeIfNeeded() before reading, as upstream's accept path did. Its ShutdownWrite now sends close_notify before the FIN, where upstream's forwarded straight to the raw socket.

resolve() gains a documented duty upstream did not state: an implementation that suspends must honour the awaiting flow's stop token, resuming it on its loop with core::async::OperationCancelled and discarding the answer that arrives later. A dial's budget and whenAny(connect, delay) both end resolution that way. A test fake that parks must honour it too, or a bounded dial through it hangs.
its code is NetErrorCode::AddressError (address resolution or parsing failed), as NetError.hpp defines it; a branch that matched AddressNotAvail for a failed lookup must match AddressError.

AllowAccept() and OnConnectionStarted() are ONE call now: tryAdmit() decides and counts in a single atomic step, so two loops cannot both be admitted to the last slot. It returns std::optional<AdmissionLease>; hold the lease for the connection's life. `if (p.AllowAccept()) { p.OnConnectionStarted(); ... }` becomes `if (auto lease = p.tryAdmit()) { ... }`.
folded into tryAdmit(), which counts the connection as it admits it; see the AllowAccept row. Delete the call.

the AdmissionLease that tryAdmit() returned ends the connection when it is destroyed, exactly once on every path. Delete the call and let the lease go out of scope (or move it into whatever owns the connection). An unmatched OnConnectionEnded() used to wrap the counter to SIZE_MAX.

the cap is fixed at construction: SetMax wrote a plain field that accepting threads read, which is a data race, and a cap changed under live connections has no answer for the ones already over it. A reload constructs a new CountingAdmissionControl for the loops that start after it.

core-cpp listeners own their own bind sequence (PosixListener::bind, IocpListener::bind), so a second one would be a second answer to who owns an address. listen(loop, ListenOptions) is the entry point.
the return type of BindAndListen; see that row.
IListener::boundPort answers this for a listener, and adoptListener asks getsockname for an adopted handle. There is no caller left holding a bare socket to ask about.
ISocket::peerAddress answers it; the sockets capture the peer when they are constructed.

Port sharing is a field of the listener's options now: listen(loop, ListenOptions { ..., .sharing = PortSharing::Shared }) sets SO_REUSEPORT on Linux, the BSDs and macOS, so one listener per loop can bind the same port. On Windows it is refused with NetErrorCode::Unsupported, because SO_REUSEADDR there lets a later socket take the port over rather than share it. The default is PortSharing::Exclusive.
